title: Area of the Longest Diagonal
statement:
You get a list rects of rectangles, where rects[i] = [length, width].

Find the rectangle with the longest diagonal and return its area. If several rectangles share the longest diagonal, return the largest area among them.

examples.why: Squared diagonals are 81 + 4 = 85 and 36 + 36 = 72. The first wins, even though the square has the bigger area.
Both squared diagonals are 50. On a tie the larger area, 25, is returned.
The 10 × 1 strip has squared diagonal 101, just above the 100 of the other two.

hints: One pass is enough. What do you compare, and what do you keep?
The diagonal is √(l² + w²). You do not need the square root to compare two diagonals.
Keep the best squared diagonal and the best area. Replace both on a strictly longer diagonal; on an equal one, keep the larger area.

explain.intuition:
By Pythagoras the diagonal of an l × w rectangle is √(l² + w²). Since the square root only grows with its input, comparing l² + w² gives the same order and stays in exact integers.

The rest is a running "best so far" with a two-level comparison: first the squared diagonal, then the area to break ties. It is the same shape as sorting a table by one column and then a second column.
steps: For each [l, w]: compute d = l² + w² and a = l · w.
If d > bestDiag, take both d and a. If d = bestDiag, set bestArea = max(bestArea, a).
pitfalls: Returning the largest area overall. A long thin rectangle can have the longest diagonal and a small area.
Comparing floating-point square roots. Equal diagonals can come out unequal after rounding, which breaks the tie rule.
Keeping the first rectangle on a tie instead of the one with the larger area.

solutions.title: Sort by diagonal, then area
solutions.idea: Sort a copy by squared diagonal descending and area descending; the first entry is the answer.

solutions.title: Single pass with squared diagonals
solutions.idea: Keep the best squared diagonal and its area; break ties by the larger area.

followups: Return the index of the chosen rectangle instead, with the smallest index on a full tie.
The rectangles are boxes with three sides. What changes in the comparison?
